::: {.callout-note title="Chapter overview"}
One set of records can owe several answers, and multiple regression is
the model behind most of them. This chapter first writes the multiple
regression model, says what a partial slope compares, and draws a
simulated process with two predictors. It then fits the model to the
98 occupations of Chapter 7 that have a recorded type, attaches
uncertainty to the education slope and checks the model, computes a
fitted profile and an average over named profiles, and compares two
prediction rules on held-out occupations. It closes with a short report
that owes three answers, a marginal description, a conditional
association and a prediction comparison, and reads and evaluates them.
By the end you will be able to write, fit and read an additive multiple
regression in R, keep changes of records, comparison, coefficient
coordinates and uncertainty calculation apart, judge a held-out
comparison, and evaluate coordinated answers without merging them.
:::

A report on occupational income may ask whether education and income move
together, whether that relationship remains when other characteristics of
the occupations are held constant, and whether those characteristics help
predict income. The questions inform one another, but answering one does
not answer the other two.

We use a **retrospective teaching study written for this chapter**. Its
records are the *Prestige* data distributed with the carData package
[@carData2022; @fox2019], whose documentation describes the data; the
analyses and the short report are ours.

A simple regression models an outcome with one predictor,
$Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i$. Multiple regression keeps that
form and adds one term for each further predictor.

## Model Formulation and Interpretation {#sec-ch8-comparisons}

### The population and observation forms

With several predictors, the model for an outcome is

$$
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{p-1}+\varepsilon,
$$

$$
E(\varepsilon\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{p-1})=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{p-1})=\sigma^2;
$$

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{i,p-1}+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
$$

The part $\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{p-1}$ is the mean of
$Y$ among units that share those predictor values, and the error
$\varepsilon$ collects everything else. The model has $p$
coefficients, counting the intercept. $\beta_0$, the intercept, is the
mean when every predictor is zero; it anchors the equation and
describes real units only if that combination is plausible within the
data. $\beta_j$, a partial slope, is the difference in the mean of $Y$
for a one-unit difference in $x_j$, holding the other predictors
fixed. $\sigma$ is the typical spread of outcomes around the mean at
fixed predictor values. The conditions apply at every combination of
predictor values: the errors average zero and
share one variance $\sigma^2$; they are independent of one another,
which comes from how the data arose; and for the exact $t$ reference
they are Normal. The intervals used here require independent errors, the classical SE
also needs the common variance, and the exact $t$ also needs Normal
errors; the HC3 covariance of Section 3.3 relaxes the common variance
under its own large-sample conditions.

Under the Normal-error model, $Y_i$ at its fixed predictor values is
Normal with mean $\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\beta_jx_{ij}$ and SD
$\sigma$. Estimating $p$ coefficients leaves $n-p$ residual degrees of
freedom. A factor with $J$ categories contributes $J-1$ indicator
columns, as Section 2.3 explains using the occupation records.

### What a partial slope compares {#ch08-several-controls}

Take two predictors, $x$ and $z$. The model mean is
$\mu(x,z)=\beta_0+\beta_Xx+\beta_Zz$. Comparing two means a unit apart
in $x$ at the same $z$ gives

$$
\mu(x+1,z)-\mu(x,z)=\beta_X(x+1)-\beta_Xx=\beta_X.
$$

All the shared terms cancel. Holding constant names this comparison of
model means; it does not mean that $x$ was changed experimentally, that
two observed units match on everything else, or that unmeasured
differences have been controlled. A partial slope's meaning belongs to
its named conditioning set. The same predictor can have a different
coefficient when a different set is held fixed. The **additive** form
also makes its comparison the same at every value of the other
predictors; Chapter 10 asks when that comparison itself varies.

Partial correlation holds variables fixed another way, by
residualizing: it removes their fitted linear parts from two variables
before correlating what remains. A fitted equation with
several predictors holds the others fixed directly, because two of its
fitted means that differ in one predictor share every other term;
Section 3.1 shows that the two routes give the same slope. Chapter 9,
Section 2, applies the same idea to adjusted group means in the
analysis of covariance.

### Simulating and graphing a two-predictor model

A known process makes the comparison concrete. Suppose

$$
Y=50+2X+5Z+\varepsilon,
\qquad E(\varepsilon\mid X,Z)=0,
$$

with finite variances and
$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)/\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.65$.
The conditional $X$ coefficient is 2, and the marginal linear slope is

$$
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
=2+5\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
=2+5(0.65)=5.25.
$$

Generate independent standard Normal values $X$ and $U$, let
$Z=.65X+\sqrt{1-.65^2}U$, and add independent Normal errors with SD 6.
Both predictors then have variance one and correlation .65.
@fig-ch8-known-process draws one generated sample of 250 cases from this
process, with the process's own mean lines rather than fitted ones. Each
solid line holds $Z$ at one value and rises 2 for each unit of $X$. The
dashed marginal line rises 5.25, because higher $X$ comes with higher $Z$
(the darker points sit toward the upper right) and the marginal line
carries that association along.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}

Three parallel solid lines at Z equal to minus one, zero and one rise with slope 2. A steeper dashed line, the marginal line, rises with slope 5.25 and crosses the three solid lines.' width=585.6}

:::


With these generated columns named `x`, `z` and `y` in `sim`, the
following calls estimate the marginal and conditional equations. The
short examples throughout this chapter show the statistical operation
on the data just described.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
coef(lm(y ~ x, data = sim))
coef(lm(y ~ x + z, data = sim))
```
:::


In this sample the fitted $X$ coefficient is 3.0259 (SE 0.5325), the
$Z$ coefficient 4.3991 (SE 0.5282), and the marginal slope 5.9971
(SE 0.4466). Each lies within two SEs of its programmed value, 2, 5,
and 5.25 respectively. A single sample estimates the process rather
than reproducing its parameters exactly.

Mapping `x` and `y` to position and `z` to colour draws the points in
@fig-ch8-known-process. The fitted slopes and the known process lines
answer related but distinct questions.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(sim, aes(x, y, colour = z)) + geom_point()
```
:::


The two slopes answer different questions: one holds $Z$ fixed, the
other includes how $Z$ moves with $X$, and neither alone says what would
happen if someone intervened on $X$. Calling 5.25 "biased" requires
naming the target it is used for; as the marginal linear slope it is
correct. Appendix A gives the derivation and the repeated samples.

## Estimating the Model on the Occupation Records {#sec-ch8-questions}

### The records and the working model

A row is an **occupation**, not a worker. Income is the occupation's
average annual income in 1971 Canadian dollars, divided here by 1,000;
education is average years of education; *women* is the percentage of
women; prestige is a rating from a mid-1960s survey, earlier than the
1971 income and education; and type is blue-collar (*bc*),
professional/managerial/technical (*prof*), or white-collar (*wc*). These
historical occupational averages are not current individual earnings.

Chapter 7 used all 102 occupations. The full variable set leaves 98
complete records, because athletes, newsboys, babysitters, and farmers
have no recorded type; the three types keep 44, 31, and 23 records. We
keep the source row order, which also makes the validation split of
Section 6 reproducible. The original 102 records are `d0`; `dat` holds
the 98 complete records, with `income_k` in thousand dollars and type
levels ordered `bc`, `prof`, `wc`.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(original = nrow(d0), retained = nrow(dat))
table(dat$type)
```
:::


We refit the education-only model on these **same 98 records** before any
adjusted comparison, so that the move from 102 to 98, a change in which
records are described, is never presented as an adjustment effect.
Complete records make the computations comparable; they do not make the
omitted occupations irrelevant or the 98 a probability sample of Canadian
occupations.

The working occupation model is

$$
\mathrm{income}_k=\beta_0+\beta_Ee+\beta_Pp+\beta_Ww
+\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}D_{\mathrm{prof}}+\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}D_{\mathrm{wc}}
+\varepsilon,
$$

where $e$ is education, $p$ prestige, $w$ percentage of women, and each
indicator $D$ is 1 for its named type. Blue-collar, with both indicators
zero, is the reference type. There are six coefficients. The
conditional question concerns $\beta_E$, comparing education at the same
prestige, women and type. Least squares describes the recorded
occupations whether or not that stochastic model holds; Section 3
applies its conditions to attach uncertainty.

A **best linear projection**, summarizing a curved relationship over a
stated predictor distribution, is a different declared target, not a
rescue adopted after curvature appears. Chapter 9, Appendix A,
develops it.

### Least squares and the fits on the same rows

Least squares chooses the coefficients that make the residual sum of
squares smallest. Its residual SD,
$s_e=\sqrt{RSS/(n-p)}$, describes the typical residual size; the full
model below gives 2.6187 thousand dollars on 92 df. $R^2$ is the share
of centered outcome variation accounted for in these records; Appendix B
introduces its adjusted version.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m0 <- lm(income_k ~ education, data = dat)
m_w <- lm(income_k ~ education + women, data = dat)
m1 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige, data = dat)
m2 <- lm(income_k ~ education + prestige + women + type, data = dat)
coef(m_w)
```

### Indicators and a fitted profile

A three-level factor needs two indicators. With blue-collar as reference,
$D_{\mathrm{prof}}$ and $D_{\mathrm{wc}}$ identify the other types;
the full occupation fit is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\mathrm{income}}_k
={}&0.4205+0.1164e+0.1406p-0.0535w\\
 &+0.3242D_{\mathrm{prof}}+0.2353D_{\mathrm{wc}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Subtract two fitted means one education year apart at the same prestige,
percentage of women and type. Every term except education cancels:

$$
\widehat m(e+1,p,w,t)-\widehat m(e,p,w,t)=\widehat\beta_E=0.1164.
$$

Thus two such occupations differ by about 116 dollars in fitted income.
At the same values of all the other predictors, a prestige point compares
about 141 dollars more, and a percentage point more women compares about
54 dollars less. Each sentence names what is held fixed.

For a white-collar profile with education 11, prestige 45, and women 50,
$D_{\mathrm{prof}}=0$ and $D_{\mathrm{wc}}=1$, and the unrounded fitted
coefficients give

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat m_*
={}&\widehat\beta_0+11\widehat\beta_E+45\widehat\beta_P
+50\widehat\beta_W+\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{wc}}\\
\approx{}&5.5886,
\end{aligned}
$$

a fitted mean of about 5,589 dollars on the historical income scale, not
a guarantee for any occupation or worker.

The intercept refers to zero education, prestige, and women in the
reference type; it anchors the fitted surface and need not describe a
plausible occupation. Nor is one type coefficient "the effect of
occupational type". When a factor stands alone, each coefficient is a
difference between group means; here each type
coefficient compares fitted means at the same education, prestige, and
women. Appendix A gives the group-mean and releveling calculations, and
Chapter 9 develops contrasts, block tests, and the analysis-of-variance
identity.

The substitution uses six multipliers, one for each coefficient.

occupations and for the declared profile. The first multiplier is 1
because every fitted value includes the intercept. A professional
record selects the professional coefficient, a white-collar record the

This gives a concrete meaning to the vector notation. Write the
multipliers as the column vector
$\mathbf x_i=(1,e_i,p_i,w_i,D_{\mathrm{prof},i},D_{\mathrm{wc},i})^{\mathsf T}$
and the corresponding coefficients as
$\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_E,\beta_P,\beta_W,
\delta_{\mathrm{prof}},\delta_{\mathrm{wc}})^{\mathsf T}$.
A **vector** is an ordered collection of numbers; the superscript
$\mathsf T$ denotes the transpose, which turns a column into a row.
The product $\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta$ adds the six
multiplier--coefficient products, exactly as the scalar equation does.

Stacking the 98 observed rows gives the $98\times6$ **design matrix**
$\mathbf X$. Stacking the outcomes and errors gives the compact model
$\mathbf Y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon$.
The design matrix stores predictors and indicators, not income. Distinct
coefficients require that no column be an exact linear combination of
the others, the **full-column-rank condition**. Near collinearity affects
precision, as Section 4.2 explains. The
profile is a new row for prediction, not an extra record used to fit
the model. `model.matrix()` recovers the observed multiplier rows;
multiplying `row` by the fitted coefficients recovers the profile mean.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rows <- c("nursing.aides", "gov.administrators", "medical.technicians")
model.matrix(m2)[rows, ]
row <- c(1, 11, 45, 50, 0, 1)
sum(row * coef(m2))
```
:::


Section 5 uses this notation to carry coefficient uncertainty to the
profile; Chapter 9, Appendix A, develops the matrix mathematics. Section 4.2 checks whether the three continuous values of that white-collar
profile occur together, using a weighted combination of observed records.

## Inference for the Partial Slope {#sec-ch8-estimate}

Apply Section 1.1's model to the occupation records: incomes vary
independently around the linear mean of Section 2.1 at the recorded
predictor rows, with a common error SD $\sigma$. The residual SD 2.6187
estimates it on 92 df. The repetition imagined for the classical
intervals is new incomes at the same 98 predictor rows; the historical
records do not establish that model or a probability sample.

### The partial slope from residuals {#ch08-partial-regression}

The partial slope can be recovered by removing the fitted parts of
the other predictors from both variables. Regress education on
prestige, percentage of women, and type and keep the residuals
$r_{E,i}$; do the same for income to obtain $r_{Y,i}$. Both auxiliary
fits include an intercept and use exactly the 98 rows of the full fit.
Then

$$
b_E=\frac{\sum_i r_{E,i}r_{Y,i}}{\sum_i r_{E,i}^2}
    =r_{EY\cdot Z}\frac{s_{r_Y}}{s_{r_E}},
$$

where $Z$ denotes the control columns and $r_{EY\cdot Z}$, the
correlation of the two residual vectors, is the partial correlation. The
numerator is the linear co-variation left after the controls and the
denominator the education variation left; the ratio of residual SDs turns
the unit-free correlation into thousand dollars per education year.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
r_E <- residuals(lm(education ~ prestige + women + type, data = dat))
r_Y <- residuals(lm(income_k ~ prestige + women + type, data = dat))
sum(r_E * r_Y) / sum(r_E^2)
```
:::


The uncertainty must count the fitted controls. Prestige and women supply
one column each and type two, so with education and the intercept the
model estimates $p=6$ coefficients from $n=98$ rows, leaving $n-p=92$
residual degrees of freedom. Using the residual variance $s_e^2=RSS/(n-p)$ of Section 2.2,

$$
SE(b_E)=\sqrt{\frac{s_e^2}
                         {\sum_i r_{E,i}^2}},
\qquad
t_E=r_{EY\cdot Z}\sqrt{\frac{n-p}{1-r_{EY\cdot Z}^2}}.
$$

The slope identity is algebraic; the SE and the $t_{92}$ reference for
$H_0:\beta_E=0$ rest on the classical model of Section 1.1. In
@tbl-ch8-partial-df the first row is the full model's education row,
which these formulas reproduce, and the second is a fresh fit of residual
income on residual education.

### Interval and tests

With 92 residual degrees of freedom, the classical 95% interval for
education is

$$
\begin{aligned}
b_E\pm t_{.975,92}SE(b_E)
 &=0.1164\pm1.9861(0.2752)\\
 &\approx[-0.4302,\ 0.6631].
\end{aligned}
$$

Under the classical assumptions the interval is compatible with negative
and positive conditional slopes, including differences of several
hundred dollars per year of education. With no margin of practical
equivalence declared, the direction and the practically relevant size
remain unresolved; the interval does not show that the slope is zero or
that adjustment has removed an effect of education.


::: {.cell}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
education -0.4301895 0.6630567
```

:::

```{.r .cell-code}
coef(m2)["education"] + c(-1, 1) * qt(.975, 92) * hc3_se
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -0.6429122  0.8757794
```

SE 0.3823 and, with the same $t_{92}$ convention, the approximate

the same Normal-error conditions as the coefficient tests,
its statistic is

$$
F_{\mathrm{overall}}=
\frac{RegSS/(p-1)}{RSS/(n-p)},
\qquad RegSS=\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\bar y)^2.
$$

```
32.1747  5.0000 92.0000
```

Not every change to a model changes the scientific estimand. In a
randomized study, well-specified covariate adjustment can estimate the

and a different uncertainty estimator changes the interval but not the

## Checking the Model {#sec-ch8-check}

What would these plots look like if the working model described the
data well? A fit produces numbers even when its mean or uncertainty
model is unsuitable. Checking asks which part of the interpretation the
evidence supports; no single graph passes or fails the model.

### Residuals, leverage, and influence

A residual is an observed deviation from a fitted value, not the
unobserved error. Leverage measures how unusual a record's combination
of predictor values is; a high-leverage record pulls the fit toward
itself, so its residual tends to be smaller. A standardized residual
therefore divides each residual by its own estimated SD, which combines
the common residual scale with the record's leverage, and an externally
studentized residual does the same with the scale estimated with that
record left out. Influence, measured by Cook's distance, combines
leverage with the size of the residual [@cook1977]. This call lists
the five occupations with the largest Cook's distance.

## The Held-Out Prediction Question {#sec-ch8-prediction}

### Learning rules and the loss

A learning rule says how training records become a prediction equation.
Our two rules are fixed: education-only OLS, and the full additive OLS
equation with education, prestige, women, and type. OLS **fits** by
minimizing squared training errors; we separately choose the **mean
absolute error (MAE)** to evaluate the predictions in income units.

A prediction opportunity here is a hypothetical same-source occupation
whose predictors are all available before its income is used, not a
forecast from information that arrives later. The records cannot show
that this exchangeability holds for other countries, periods, individual
workers, or types absent from the dictionary.

For held-out outcomes $y_i$ and predictions $\widehat y_i^{(-)}$ fitted
without those outcomes,

$$
MAE=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
       \sum_{i\in\mathrm{test}}\left|y_i-\widehat y_i^{(-)}\right|.
$$

A smaller MAE means a smaller average absolute error on the evaluated
cases, not a better prediction for every case.

### Shared ten-fold validation

In shared ten-fold cross-validation the 98 records are divided into ten
folds, and each fold takes a turn as the held-out set: both rules are
fitted to the other records and predict the held-out cases
(@fig-ch8-folds), and the 98 case-level errors are then pooled.
@tbl-ch8-validation records the protocol.

### Functions and traces in the report

Reading starts by locating what each passage does. In Chapter 1's
terms, a component is a logical function, such as STAT-E or SUB-J, and
the report's study-specific content serves it. One passage can serve
several functions. R0, for example, identifies the records for STAT-E
and supplies their historical context for SUB-E. It would become
justification (J) content only if it offered a reason connecting those
records to an inference; "we used R" offers none. @tbl-ch8-traces lists
each function once, with the content shared by the three pairs and the
content specific to each.

| Function | Shared or pair-specific content | Trace in this teaching record |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **STAT-E** | Named 98 rows, variables, exclusions, and computations' inputs | R0; the row audit and import code in @sec-ch8-questions |
| **SUB-E** | Occupations rather than workers; historical dollars, education, ratings, and types | R0; variable/source descriptions |
| **STAT-J** | Pair 1: fixed-record least-squares definition. Pair 2: declared stochastic model and uncertainty conditions. Pair 3: held-out fitting, fixed rules, loss, and exchangeability | R1--R3; model declaration; validation protocol and code |
| **SUB-J** | Reasons connecting those measurements and comparisons to historical occupational income, with limits on individual, current, and causal interpretations | R0--R3; unit/time explanations and prediction-opportunity definition |
| **STAT-I** | Pair 1's 0.8830 slope; Pair 2's 0.1164 estimate, intervals, coefficient test and checks; Pair 3's case-level errors, MAEs, and split sensitivity | @sec-ch8-estimate through @sec-ch8-prediction; R1--R3 |
| **STAT-C** | Descriptive positive marginal slope; unresolved conditional slope under the model; smaller internal error for the full rule under the protocol | R1, R2, and R3 respectively |
| **SUB-I** | Interpret years, income units, conditioning, and prediction errors in the named historical occupation setting | Worked substitutions and error calculation; R1--R3 |
| **SUB-C** | Each question-facing answer with its own limits; none supplies a causal or individual-earnings answer | R1--R3; their distinctions preserved in R4 |

SUB-E situates the evidence, SUB-J **augments and contextualizes** the
statistical justification, SUB-I interprets the inference, and SUB-C
bounds the substantive answer. Sharing a dataset does not make Pair 2's
independent-error model into Pair 3's validation procedure.

For each supporting statement, record what the report says and where
the reader finds it: in the report, the data documentation, or the
executable calculations. Gaps and conflicts are stated in ordinary
prose. R2 states the independence assumption, for example, but nothing in
the record shows that independence holds under the original selection of
occupations; a stated assumption and evidence for it are different
information. The unit conversion, by contrast, makes reading 0.883
thousand dollars as about 883 dollars traceable. This record contains no
conflicting source, though a real study may contain incompatible
descriptions to record and investigate. A reason's documentary status is
simply what has been stated or located and which support is missing; it
is not a quality score or a set of categories to learn.

Professional knowledge helps identify a trace's function but does not
license adding an unreported design feature. An invalid reason such as
"all rows are in the same dataset, therefore they are independent" is
still **stated J**, whose adequacy is judged separately: reading records
the reason actually offered, not a repaired one.

### Evaluating each answer

Evaluation now judges the quality of the reasoning just identified.
Chapter 1's six questions apply to each argument (@tbl-ch8-quality); they
are not six scores to total.

| Quality-evaluation question | Application to these arguments |
|:--|:--|
| **Question alignment** | R1 matches its finite-record slope. R2 names $\beta_E$, its fitted estimate, the conditioning set, and the model extension. R3 names the learning procedure, loss, and training sizes rather than substituting a coefficient test. |
| **Evidence integrity** | The 102-to-98 accounting and common rows are explicit. Missing type still limits what is represented. CV excludes held-out outcomes from fitting; source selection is not repaired by that procedure. |
| **Justification adequacy** | Least squares is sufficient for the declared finite description. Pair 2's model conditions and Pair 3's same-source exchangeability remain assumptions with incomplete empirical support. Statistical computation alone cannot establish them. |
| **Inferential adequacy** | The slope, intervals, error arithmetic, and comparisons are reproducible. Neither zero-crossing nor a large p-value proves absence; repeated folds are not independent replication. Substantive reasoning must retain those distinctions. |
| **Transition fidelity** | Occupation-level average income remains occupation-level average income; partial adjustment is not a causal intervention, and model fit is not held-out performance. |
| **Claim calibration** | R1 remains finite and historical; R2 reports unresolved magnitude/direction rather than no relationship; R3 remains internal and procedure-specific. No claim extends to individual workers or modern populations. |

: Apply the six questions before evaluating the study-level synthesis. {#tbl-ch8-quality tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

Chapter 1 distinguishes judgments about a reason from the conclusion
about a whole question--answer pair. Here the finite description is
**supported as stated**; the explicitly unresolved conditional answer is
also **supported as stated**, under its disclosed model limits. A
correctly reported inconclusive answer need not establish a stronger
claim to be supported. The prediction comparison is supported as a
qualified internal result, while external superiority of the final

### Is the synthesis coherent?

Coordinated questions add one evaluation question, **Cross-question
coherence**: does the synthesis preserve the distinct questions,
estimands, methods, analytic statuses, uncertainty, and limits of the
separate answers? We introduce it here; Argument Chapter B develops it
further but is not needed to apply it.

R4 reports a positive marginal slope, an unresolved conditional slope,
and better internal prediction. **Predict and explain:** can an interval
that includes zero for the education coefficient coexist with a lower
held-out MAE for the full rule? Identify the question each result
answers before reading this alternative synthesis:

> Once the other predictors were controlled, education had no effect;
> nevertheless, the significant full regression proves it will predict
> workers' incomes accurately.

The results can coexist: the interval concerns one conditional
coefficient, whereas the rules differ by prestige, women and type
together. Better predictions from the full rule do not isolate
education's contribution. R4 retains these distinct answers.

Reading first identifies the inference and claim the alternative offers. Evaluation
then finds three failures: "no effect" substitutes a causal null for the
conditional-association answer, an omnibus significance test is not
held-out validation, and occupations have become workers. The corrected
synthesis is R4, not a fourth overarching argument that erases the
separate conclusions.

These records were collected for earlier purposes, not prospectively
for our three teaching questions. Chapter 1's repair-versus-new-cycle
rule applies: correcting an error under the same target is a repair;
choosing a causal target after seeing an association is a revised or
new cycle whose timing must be stated. Argument Chapter B, Section 5,
develops the full coordinated construction workflow.

## Reading Bridge {#sec-ch8-summary}

Start with a model naming its outcome, predictors, coefficients and
error variation. The known process showed partial slopes at fixed other
predictors before the occupation records supplied estimates. Multiple
regression adds conditional comparisons without conferring automatic
causal control. Subtracting fitted means showed what a coefficient compares;
residualizing connected it to covariance; residual, influence, support,
and precision checks each bounded the answer differently; a fitted
profile and a standardized average extended the conditional model; and
held-out errors answered a separately owed question. The occupation study
owed three answers, a finite-record marginal description, a working-model
conditional interval with unresolved magnitude, and a qualified internal
prediction comparison, and its shared records made the questions
coordinated without making their justifications identical. Chapter 9 develops extensions of this model (factors with several levels and their
contrasts, nested model comparison and information criteria, changed
predictor and outcome forms, and robust, clustered, and bootstrap
uncertainty) and transfers the reading to Project STAR, where a
randomized design supplies a different warrant. Chapter 10 then extends
the interaction reasoning of Chapters 4 and 6 to regression.

### Key terms {.unnumbered}

Use this short reference to revisit the concepts introduced here. The
Part One Concept Reference gives the broader reference and the principal home
of each concept; the simple-regression, interval, ANOVA, and reading
vocabulary used in this chapter is explained in Chapters 1--4 and 7.

| Term and common alternatives | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| Multiple regression (multiple regression model; additive model) | A model in which an outcome's mean is an intercept plus one term per predictor, $E(Y\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{p-1})=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{p-1}$, with errors of one common SD $\sigma$; its $p$ coefficients leave $n-p$ residual df, and least squares estimates them. Each coefficient compares means at the same values of the other predictors; the additive form assumes each comparison is the same across those values. |
| Partial slope (conditional coefficient; adjusted coefficient) | The difference in fitted outcome per one-unit difference in one predictor, holding the model's other predictors fixed. Its meaning depends on the conditioning set named with it; it is not an intervention effect or a claim about unmeasured differences. |
| Indicator variable (dummy variable) and reference category | A 0/1 variable marking membership in one category of a factor; a factor with $J$ levels needs $J-1$ indicators, and the omitted level is the reference. The intercept refers to the reference category; each indicator coefficient is a difference from it at the same other predictors. Releveling changes coordinates, not fitted values. |
| Partial regression (residualization; added-variable form) | Regressing both the outcome and one predictor on the other predictors, then relating their residuals. The residual slope equals the partial slope; the residual correlation is the partial correlation, unit-free. |
| Coefficient covariance matrix | The estimated variances and covariances of the fitted coefficients (`vcov()` in R). Any linear combination of coefficients, such as a fitted mean or a contrast, has variance $\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf c$; adding SEs or ignoring covariances is a different, incorrect calculation. |
| Variance inflation factor (VIF) | One divided by one minus the $R^2$ from regressing a predictor on the other predictors. Its square root multiplies that coefficient's SE relative to an orthogonal design, holding residual variance fixed; it describes precision, not bias, and is not a deletion rule. |
| Joint support (covariate hull) | Whether a combination of predictor values lies within the region where observations actually occur, not merely within each variable's separate range. A fitted value outside joint support is extrapolation even if each coordinate is observed somewhere. |
| Standardization over a named distribution (model-averaged fitted value) | Averaging the model's fitted values after setting one predictor to a chosen value for every profile in a declared set with fixed weights. Its uncertainty uses the coefficient covariance; it is not an observed group mean, a causal effect, or held-out performance. |
| Learning rule (learning procedure) | A fixed recipe that turns training records into a prediction equation, such as fitting a declared OLS formula. Prediction performance concerns the rule at stated training sizes, not one final fitted equation. |
| Cross-validation (held-out validation) | Dividing records into folds, fitting a rule on the other folds, predicting the held-out fold, and pooling the errors so that no outcome contributes to its own prediction. Resplits describe sensitivity to the partition, not new independent studies. |
| Mean absolute error (MAE) | The average absolute difference between held-out outcomes and their predictions, in outcome units. It is an evaluation loss chosen separately from the squared-error criterion that OLS minimizes. |
| Cross-question coherence | The additional evaluation question for coordinated answers: does the synthesis preserve the distinct questions, estimands, methods, uncertainty, and limits of the separate answers rather than merging them into one omnibus claim? |

### Why the marginal slope includes another association {.unnumbered}

Suppose a population process is

$$
Y=\beta_0+\beta_X X+\beta_Z Z+\varepsilon,
\qquad E(\varepsilon\mid X,Z)=0,
$$

with finite variances and $\operatorname{Var}(X)>0$. The marginal
least-squares slope is a covariance divided by a variance. Substituting
the outcome equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
&=\frac{\beta_X\operatorname{Var}(X)
+\beta_Z\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)
+\operatorname{Cov}(X,\varepsilon)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\\
&=\beta_X+\beta_Z
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch8a-omission}

The zero-error-covariance condition removes the final term. The sample
counterpart holds exactly for least-squares fits on the same rows, as
Section 2.2's prestige and women calculations show. The
discrepancy therefore involves both the association between $X$ and $Z$
and $Z$'s coefficient in the outcome model; neither ingredient alone
determines its size. If the target is the conditional coefficient,
omitting $Z$ creates bias relative to that target. If the target is the
marginal slope, that marginal quantity is not a biased version of an
unstated conditional target. The two coefficients name different
comparisons, and neither supplies a causal warrant for observational
variables.

Y=50+2X+5Z+\varepsilon.
$$ {#eq-ch8a-sim-process}

### Fitted group means from indicators {.unnumbered}

Start with a model containing only the three-level type factor. With
blue-collar as reference,

$$

\widehat\delta_{\mathrm{prof}}D_{\mathrm{prof}}+

### Cook's distance {.unnumbered}

With $p$ coefficient columns including the intercept, leverage is
$h_{ii}=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf x_i$. Cook's distance can be calculated as

$$
D_i=\frac{e_i^2}{p s^2}\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}
=\frac{(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(-i)})^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X
(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(-i)})}{p s^2}.
$$

The second expression measures the change in all coefficients when
record $i$ is deleted, in the design matrix's metric rather than as an
unweighted sum of squared coefficients with incompatible units.

### The HC3 covariance {.unnumbered}

For independent observations, the HC3 covariance estimator is

$$
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{HC3}}=(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\left\{\sum_i \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\frac{e_i^2}{(1-h_{ii})^2}\right\}
(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1}.
$$

The outer factors are the familiar design component. The middle
component lets each record carry its own residual scale, inflated for
leverage [@long2000; @zeileis2004]. The OLS coefficients do not change;
only their covariance does, as @tbl-ch8b-hc3 shows for all six
coefficients; `vcovHC()` evaluates this covariance calculation.

### VIF and generalized VIF {.unnumbered}

For a single predictor column, the classical conditional variance of its
coefficient can be written

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_j\mid\mathbf X)=
\frac{\sigma^2}{\sum_i(X_{ij}-\bar X_j)^2}
\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}.
$$

Here $R_j^2$ comes from regressing that predictor on the remaining
columns, including the intercept. The variance inflation factor is
$VIF_j=1/(1-R_j^2)$, and its square root is an SE multiplier, holding the
residual variance and the focal predictor's variation fixed
[@kutner2005]. Education gives $R_j^2=.8765$, VIF 8.0968, and SE
multiplier 2.8455 (Section 4.2), from the auxiliary regression or
`car::vif(m2)`. The education--prestige
correlation is .8665, but the VIF uses all the other columns, not just
that pair.

The two-column type term has a generalized VIF. Its raw GVIF is 7.7001;
the dimension-adjusted value $GVIF^{1/(2\,df)}=1.6658$ is on a scale
comparable to the square root of a one-column VIF [@fox2019], whereas the
raw two-column GVIF is not comparable with an ordinary one-column VIF.

Exact collinearity makes the design rank-deficient. Near collinearity
leaves the coefficients estimable but possibly imprecise, and under the
maintained zero-conditional-mean model it does not by itself bias OLS. A
cutoff of 5 or 10 neither establishes the model's assumptions nor
justifies removing a variable the question requires. Measurement problems
need their own evidence: the familiar attenuation story requires
classical error assumptions and is not a rule for every coefficient in a
multiple-predictor model.

### The Normal likelihood, AIC, and BIC {.unnumbered}

Chapter 6 varied the candidate probability for a fixed binomial count of
32 successes in 50 trials. Here the data again stay fixed, but the
response is continuous and the parameters are several coefficients plus
an error scale. For a declared independent Normal linear model, the
**likelihood** is the joint density of the observed outcomes at their
fixed predictor values, viewed as a function of those parameters; it is
not a probability assigned to a parameter, nor the probability of the
exact observed vector. The **log-likelihood** adds the log densities of
the independent records.

Write the predictor row for record $i$ as $\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}$ and let $\sigma>0$ be the
error SD. Before fitting, the log-likelihood is

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma)=-n\log\sigma-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i(y_i-\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta)^2.
$$

At any fixed positive scale only the last term changes with the
coefficients, so maximizing over $\boldsymbol\beta$ minimizes the residual
sum of squares: the Normal maximum-likelihood coefficients equal the OLS
coefficients. This connects Chapter 7's squared-loss criterion to this
particular distributional model, although least squares did not need the
model to calculate a minimizing line.

Maximizing over the scale gives
$\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{ML}}=\sqrt{RSS/n}$, whereas the residual SD used
for classical coefficient uncertainty is $s=\sqrt{RSS/(n-p)}$, with $p$
counting the regression coefficients. The two serve different purposes,
and the ML scale, not the residual SD, belongs in the fitted likelihood.
At the fitted coefficients and ML scale,

$$
\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{ML}})
=-\frac n2\left\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(RSS/n)\right\}.
$$

R's `logLik()` returns this maximized value for an `lm()` fit: the Normal
log densities of the 98 outcomes at their fitted means and the ML scale
add to the same number. Two
information criteria combine it with a penalty for the number of
parameters:

$$
AIC=-2\log\widehat L+2k,\qquad
BIC=-2\log\widehat L+k\log n.
$$

Here $k$ counts the regression coefficients **and** the estimated
residual variance, so the full occupation model has $k=7$. Smaller values
are preferred under each criterion; neither is a held-out MAE
[@akaike1974; @schwarz1978]. For *m2* the ML scale is 2.5373 and the
residual SD 2.6187; the maximized log-likelihood is $-230.302$, so its
AIC is 474.6040 and its BIC 492.6988.

@tbl-ch8b-criteria compares the three declared models on the same 98
rows, response scale, and likelihood convention. Its adjusted $R^2$, $1-(1-R^2)(n-1)/(n-p)$,
charges each added coefficient a small penalty: it rises only when the
added terms' nested-model $F$ statistic exceeds 1. Like $R^2$, AIC and
BIC, it is computed from the fit to the same 98 rows, so it is an
in-sample summary, not a held-out measure. Chapter 11 develops likelihood
fitting further for binomial outcomes; this local Normal-model
calculation does not need it.
